title: How to Use Bond ETFs for Stable Retirement Income
description: Generating yield and stability without buying individual bonds.
content:
Bonds are the ballast of a retirement portfolio. They provide steady income (yield) and typically hold their value when stocks crash. While buying individual bonds offers precise control, it is complex and requires large capital. Bond ETFs (Exchange Traded Funds) offer instant diversification, liquidity, and monthly income payments for any budget. This guide explains the different types of Bond ETFs—Treasury, Corporate, Aggregate—and how to mix them to build a reliable income machine.

Key Takeaways

  • Aggregate vs. Specific: A 'Total Bond' fund (BND) owns everything. It is simple but exposes you to all risks. Specific funds (like SHY for Short Treasuries) allow you to target safety or yield precisely.
  • Duration Risk: The most important metric. 'Long Duration' funds (TLT) crash when interest rates rise. 'Short Duration' funds (BSV) are stable. Retirees should generally lean toward Short/Intermediate duration.
  • Monthly Income: Most Bond ETFs pay interest monthly, unlike stocks which pay quarterly. This aligns perfectly with monthly bills.
  • Defined Maturity ETFs: New products (like iBonds or BulletShares) mature on a specific date, acting like individual bonds. You get your principal back at the end, eliminating interest rate risk if held to term.

Why It Matters (US Context)

US Treasuries are state-tax free. Corporate bonds are not. Municipal bonds are federal-tax free. Choosing the right ETF for the right account (IRA vs Brokerage) allows you to keep more of your yield.

The Bond ETF Menu

Build your income floor.

1. The Anchor: Total Bond Market (BND / AGG)

Yield: ~4.5%. Duration: ~6 Years.
Role: The default core. Owns ~10,000 bonds (Govt + Corp). Good balance of risk/reward.

2. The Safety: Short-Term Treasuries (SHV / SGOV)

Yield: ~5.0%. Duration: <1 Year.
Role: Cash substitute. Almost zero volatility. Great for money needed in 1-2 years.

3. The Yield Boost: Corporate Bonds (VCIT / LQD)

Yield: ~5.5% - 6.0%.
Role: Higher income, but higher risk. In a recession, these can drop like stocks. Keep allocation modest.

4. The Inflation Fighter: TIPS (VTIP)

Yield: Inflation + Base Rate.
Role: Protects purchasing power. Essential for 30-year retirements.

Portfolio Construction

  1. The 'Safe' Slice: Keep 50% of your bond allocation in Treasuries (GOVT or VGIT). This is your recession insurance.
  2. The 'Ladder' with ETFs: Buy a 2026 BulletShare, a 2027 BulletShare, and a 2028 BulletShare. You have created a 3-year income ladder using funds. When the 2026 fund matures, it turns to cash.
  3. Asset Location: Put Corporate and Total Bond funds in your IRA. Put Treasury or Muni funds in your Taxable account. This optimizes for the specific tax treatment of the interest.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did BND lose money in 2022?

Interest rates rose from 0% to 4% rapidly. When rates rise, bond prices fall. However, the future expected return is now higher because the yield is higher. It is a short-term pain for long-term gain.

Are High Yield (Junk) bonds good?

They act like stocks. They have high correlation to the S&P 500. They do not provide good diversification benefits. Use them sparingly or not at all.

Do I lose principal?

In a standard ETF (BND), you have no maturity date, so principal fluctuates. In a Defined Maturity ETF (BulletShares), principal is returned at the end date. Use Defined Maturity for certainty.
